basics.title: What is IRR (Internal Rate of Return)
basics.p1: The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a financial metric that represents the discount rate that makes the net present value (NPV) of a series of cash flows equal to zero. In other words, it's the expected rate of return of an investment or project.
basics.p2: IRR is widely used to evaluate investment feasibility, compare different opportunities, and make financial decisions. The higher the IRR, the more attractive the investment.
basics.p3: IRR is especially useful because it considers the time value of money, recognizing that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future.

cashflows.title: Cash flows: inflows and outflows
cashflows.intro: To calculate IRR correctly, you need to identify all cash flows of the investment:

outflows.title: Outflows (negative values)
outflows.e1: Initial investment (e.g., property purchase, stock investment)
outflows.e2: Costs and expenses (e.g., maintenance, taxes, fees)

inflows.title: Inflows (positive values)
inflows.e2: Sale or redemption value at the end (e.g., property sale, investment redemption)

periodicity.title: Cash flow frequency
periodicity.intro: IRR can be calculated for different frequencies. The calculator automatically converts to equivalent annual rate:

mensal.title: Monthly
mensal.body: Cash flows occur every month. Useful for investments with monthly revenue like rent or installments.

trimestral.title: Quarterly
trimestral.body: Cash flows occur every 3 months. Common in quarterly financial reports.

semestral.title: Semiannual
semestral.body: Cash flows occur every 6 months. Used in some contracts and medium-term investments.

anual.title: Annual
anual.body: Cash flows occur once per year. Ideal for long-term projects and annual analyses.

periodicity.note: The calculator always shows the IRR in the selected period and the equivalent annual IRR to facilitate comparisons.

interpretation.title: How to interpret the IRR result
interpretation.intro: The IRR value indicates the investment's profitability:

positive.title: Positive IRR
positive.body: Indicates the investment generates returns above the opportunity cost. The higher the positive IRR, the better the investment. Compare with market interest rates or your minimum expected return rate.

negative.title: Negative IRR
negative.body: Indicates the investment is not financially viable - cash flows don't compensate for the initial investment. Consider other alternatives or review projected cash flows.

zero.title: Zero or very close to zero IRR
zero.body: Indicates the investment only recovers the invested capital, without generating additional returns. May be acceptable if the goal is capital preservation, but not ideal for growth.

disclaimer.text: This calculator is educational and provides estimates based on the cash flows entered. The actual IRR may vary due to factors such as inflation, unconsidered risks, changes in market conditions, and other external factors. Use results as an analysis tool and consult a financial professional for important decisions.

q1.question: What is IRR and what is it used for?
q1.answer: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) is the discount rate that makes the net present value of an investment equal to zero. It's used to evaluate investment profitability, compare different opportunities, and make financial decisions. The higher the IRR, the more attractive the investment.

q2.question: How to interpret a negative IRR?
q2.answer: A negative IRR indicates the investment is not financially viable - future cash flows don't compensate for the initial investment. This means you would lose money with this investment. Consider other alternatives or review projected cash flows.

q3.question: What's the difference between monthly IRR and annual IRR?
q3.answer: Monthly IRR is calculated considering cash flows occur monthly. Annual IRR is the equivalent annual rate, calculated by converting monthly IRR to an annual rate using the formula: (1 + monthly_IRR)¹² - 1. The calculator shows both to facilitate comparisons with other annual market rates.

q4.question: Can I use negative and positive values in cash flows?
q4.answer: Yes! Negative values represent money outflows (investments, expenses) and positive values represent inflows (revenue, returns). It's essential to have at least one negative flow (initial investment) and at least one positive flow (return) to calculate IRR.

q5.question: How to paste cash flows from a spreadsheet?
q5.answer: You can copy a column or row of values from a spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets) and paste directly into the cash flow field. The calculator automatically detects values separated by line breaks or tabs and imports them. Use negative values for outflows and positive values for inflows.

q6.question: Does IRR consider inflation?
q6.answer: Not directly. The calculated IRR uses the nominal values of the entered cash flows. If you want an analysis considering inflation, you should use cash flows already adjusted for expected inflation (real values). The resulting IRR will be a real rate, not nominal.

q7.question: When to use IRR vs other metrics like NPV or payback?
q7.answer: IRR is useful for comparing investments of different sizes and terms, as it shows the percentage return rate. NPV shows the absolute value in currency. Payback shows how long it takes to recover the investment. Use IRR to compare opportunities, NPV to see total value generated, and payback to evaluate liquidity.
